title: Trivia — First Bank
attribution: Original agent-drafted questions for Next Round, released under CC0-1.0; no human attestation claimed.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Japan?
questions.explanation: Tokyo has been Japan's capital since 1868; Kyoto was the imperial capital before it.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.explanation: The Sahara covers about 9.2 million square kilometres of North Africa. Antarctica is a larger desert overall, but it is a cold desert.

questions.prompt: Which of these capital cities stands on the River Danube?
questions.explanation: Vienna stands on the Danube. Prague is on the Vltava, Warsaw on the Vistula, and Berlin on the Spree.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest country in Africa by land area?
questions.explanation: Algeria covers about 2.38 million square kilometres. Sudan was larger until South Sudan became independent in 2011.

questions.prompt: Which strait separates Peninsular Malaysia from the Indonesian island of Sumatra?
questions.explanation: The Strait of Malacca runs between Malaysia and Sumatra and is one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

questions.prompt: Who was the first President of the United States?
questions.explanation: George Washington served as the first president, from 1789 to 1797.

questions.prompt: In which year did the Second World War end?
questions.explanation: The war ended in 1945, with Germany's surrender in May and Japan's in September.

questions.prompt: Which English king sealed Magna Carta in 1215?
questions.explanation: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215 under pressure from his barons.

questions.prompt: Who is credited with developing the movable-type printing press in Europe around 1440?
questions.explanation: Johannes Gutenberg's press in Mainz made mass-produced books practical in Europe.

questions.prompt: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided newly encountered lands outside Europe between which two powers?
questions.explanation: Spain and Portugal agreed on a meridian in the Atlantic: lands to the east went to Portugal, lands to the west to Spain.

questions.prompt: What is the chemical formula for water?
questions.explanation: A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.

questions.prompt: Which is the tallest land animal?
questions.explanation: An adult giraffe stands up to about 5.5 metres tall, taller than any other land animal.

questions.prompt: Which organelle is known as the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria produce most of a cell's ATP, its main energy currency.

questions.prompt: About how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
questions.explanation: Light in a vacuum travels at about 299,792 kilometres per second.

questions.prompt: Which particle, proposed in 1964, was confirmed by experiments at CERN in 2012?
questions.explanation: The ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN announced the discovery of the Higgs boson in July 2012.

questions.prompt: What does 'WWW' stand for in a web address?
questions.explanation: WWW is short for World Wide Web, the system of linked pages invented by Tim Berners-Lee.

questions.prompt: How many bits are in a byte?
questions.explanation: A byte is eight bits, enough to represent 256 different values.

questions.prompt: Who is generally regarded as the first computer programmer, for work published in the 1840s?
questions.explanation: Ada Lovelace's notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine included an algorithm for the machine, the first published computer program.

questions.prompt: Which data structure stores and retrieves items in last-in, first-out (LIFO) order?
questions.explanation: A stack adds and removes at the same end. A queue is first-in, first-out instead.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly partitions an array around a pivot element, with average-case performance of O(n log n)?
questions.explanation: Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the array around it, and recurses on each side.

questions.prompt: Who wrote the play Romeo and Juliet?
questions.explanation: William Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet in the 1590s.

questions.prompt: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.explanation: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa in the early 1500s.

questions.prompt: Which novel opens with the words 'Call me Ishmael'?
questions.explanation: Herman Melville's Moby-Dick (1851) is narrated by Ishmael, a sailor aboard the Pequod.

questions.prompt: The epic poem the Odyssey is traditionally attributed to which ancient Greek poet?
questions.explanation: The Odyssey and the Iliad are traditionally attributed to Homer. Virgil wrote the Roman epic the Aeneid.

questions.prompt: Which composer wrote the Goldberg Variations for keyboard?
questions.explanation: Bach's Goldberg Variations, published in 1741, are an aria with thirty variations for harpsichord.

questions.prompt: Which band released the album Abbey Road in 1969?
questions.explanation: Abbey Road was the last album the Beatles recorded together, released in September 1969.

questions.prompt: Who played Jack Dawson in the 1997 film Titanic?
questions.explanation: Leonardo DiCaprio played Jack, opposite Kate Winslet as Rose.

questions.prompt: Which singer was known as the 'King of Pop'?
questions.explanation: Michael Jackson was dubbed the King of Pop. Elvis Presley was the King of Rock and Roll.

questions.prompt: In The Simpsons, what is the name of the town where the Simpson family lives?
questions.explanation: The Simpsons live in Springfield; Shelbyville is its rival town.

questions.prompt: Who composed the score for the 1960 film Psycho, including the famous shrieking strings of the shower scene?
questions.explanation: Bernard Herrmann scored several Hitchcock films; Psycho's music uses strings only.

questions.prompt: How many players does a football (soccer) team field at the start of a match?
questions.explanation: A soccer team fields eleven players, including the goalkeeper.

questions.prompt: In tennis, what word is used for a score of zero?
questions.explanation: A zero score in tennis is called love, as in 'thirty-love'. A duck is a zero in cricket.

questions.prompt: Chess developed from the earlier game chaturanga, which originated in which country?
questions.explanation: Chaturanga arose in India around the 6th century; chess then spread westward through Persia.

questions.prompt: How many rings appear on the Olympic flag?
questions.explanation: The Olympic flag bears five interlaced rings, representing the inhabited continents.

questions.prompt: In algebraic chess notation, which piece is represented by the letter N?
questions.explanation: The knight is written N because K is already used for the king.

questions.prompt: Sushi is a traditional dish that originated in which country?
questions.explanation: Sushi developed in Japan as seasoned rice served with preserved fish and other toppings.

questions.prompt: What is the main ingredient in guacamole?
questions.explanation: Guacamole is mashed avocado, traditionally with lime, salt, onion, and chilli.

questions.prompt: Which variety of rice is traditionally used to make risotto?
questions.explanation: Arborio is a short-grain Italian rice whose starch gives risotto its creamy texture.

questions.prompt: Saffron, among the most expensive spices by weight, is harvested from which flower?
questions.explanation: Saffron is the dried stigma of Crocus sativus; each flower yields only three threads.

questions.prompt: The alcohol in beer and wine is produced by fermentation carried out by which organism?
questions.explanation: Yeast converts sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide during fermentation.

questions.prompt: How many letters are there in the modern English alphabet?
questions.explanation: The modern English alphabet has 26 letters, from A to Z.

questions.prompt: Which word is the best opposite (antonym) of 'ancient'?
questions.explanation: Ancient means very old; its opposite is modern. Antique and archaic are near-synonyms of ancient.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a word or phrase that reads the same forwards and backwards, such as 'level'?
questions.explanation: A palindrome reads identically in both directions. An anagram rearranges letters into a different word.

questions.prompt: Which language has the largest number of native speakers?
questions.explanation: Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers; English has more speakers overall when second-language speakers are counted.

questions.prompt: The Latin phrase 'carpe diem' comes from a poem by Horace. What does it urge the reader to do?
questions.explanation: Carpe diem, from Horace's Odes, literally means 'pluck (seize) the day'. 'Remember death' is memento mori.

questions.prompt: How many minutes are there in three hours?
questions.explanation: Three hours at sixty minutes each is 180 minutes.

questions.prompt: A silver wedding anniversary marks how many years of marriage?
questions.explanation: The 25th anniversary is silver; the 50th is golden.

questions.prompt: In the Northern Hemisphere, the autumnal equinox falls in which month?
questions.explanation: The September equinox, around 22-23 September, marks the start of northern autumn.

questions.prompt: What is the standard office paper size used in most of Europe?
questions.explanation: A4 (210 x 297 mm) is the standard office size in most of the world outside North America.

questions.prompt: Which unit of length was originally defined in the 1790s as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator?
questions.explanation: The French Academy defined the metre from the Earth's meridian; the kilometre is simply a thousand metres.
